segments.title: Henderson and British multi-carrier doctrine
segments.summary: Reginald Henderson's appointment explains how the Royal Navy organized command for coordinated carrier operations before the Second World War.
segments.body: The Royal Navy had been developing multi-carrier operations since the late 1920s and appointed Henderson as Rear Admiral, Aircraft Carriers in 1930. Coordinating carriers, battlecruisers, aircraft, and communications required a flag officer and a substantial staff. Older carriers could operate aircraft effectively but often lacked the accommodation needed to host that command organization. That shortage helps explain why senior command could remain in a battlecruiser even while the fleet was moving toward carrier-centered operations. The later accommodation disputes around Philip Vian's carrier staff illustrate why this was a practical command problem rather than an abstract organizational preference.

evidence.note: The lecture identifies Henderson's appointment, the prewar multi-carrier concept, and the flag-staff accommodation problem.

segments.title: Fleet carriers, strike carriers, and treaty tonnage
segments.summary: British carrier design traded air-group size against protection while combining armored fleet carriers with larger strike carriers such as Ark Royal.
segments.body: The intended force mixed roughly three protected fleet carriers with a strike carrier carrying a larger air group. Global commitments in the Mediterranean, Atlantic, Indian Ocean, and Far East pushed the Royal Navy toward survivable ships even when treaty tonnage limited aircraft capacity. A total allowance of about 135,000 tons made five 27,000-ton carriers inadequate for those worldwide commitments, while smaller hulls forced a choice between air-group size and armour. Courageous, Glorious, and, with qualifications, Furious supplied the older strike-carrier lineage before Ark Royal, while the later Implacable design could combine more of both roles on a larger post-treaty hull. The same design-study family also pointed toward Unicorn and the light fleet carriers. The comparison shows that armoured flight decks and smaller air groups were theatre-driven choices rather than evidence that British planners ignored offensive aviation.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the strike-carrier and fleet-carrier mix, treaty limits, armor, air groups, and Implacable lineage.

segments.title: Harbor-attack planning before Taranto
segments.summary: Taranto drew on decades of harbor intelligence, aerial-torpedo experiments, and Royal Navy frustration with enemy fleets sheltered in port.
segments.body: The exact origin of the Taranto plan is disputed, but the Royal Navy already held detailed information about the harbour before the Abyssinia Crisis. The lecture traces the operational ancestry back to First World War plans for Sopwith Cuckoo attacks on ships sheltered at Wilhelmshaven. Those plans influenced work on Eagle, Hermes, and Furious, and postwar committees continued studying harbour attack. The mature concept was a surprise night strike against a concentrated fleet when its defences and crews were least prepared. Long-term collection of publicly obtainable harbour depths and profiles turned ordinary hydrographic information into operational intelligence when war made Taranto a target. The example shows why information need not be secret to become militarily decisive when it is systematically collected and kept current.

evidence.note: The lecture links Taranto intelligence and planning to First World War harbour-attack work, carrier conversions, hydrographic collection, and the Abyssinia Crisis.

segments.title: Fleet Air Arm procurement and divided authority
segments.summary: The Navy paid for and operationally directed the Fleet Air Arm, yet requirements, careers, and engineering feedback passed through divided Admiralty-Air Ministry authority.
segments.body: Aircraft requirements travelled from fleet operators through the Admiralty and Air Ministry to manufacturers and then back through the same long chain. The Navy funded the Fleet Air Arm and exercised operational control, but disciplinary and career authority remained divided. Naval pilots could hold a Royal Navy rank and a different flying rank, creating theoretical command inversions within squadrons even when personnel resolved them pragmatically. Multiple departments magnified the risk that an operational requirement would be diluted before it reached an aircraft designer. The arrangement shows how divided financial, operational, and career control complicated an otherwise plausible attempt to centralize aviation expertise.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the procurement chain, divided Fleet Air Arm authority, and the mismatch between naval and flying ranks.

segments.title: Bomber priorities and the operator-engineer gap
segments.summary: Air Ministry concentration on bombers and weak contact between operators and engineers left other aviation roles scrambling to recover in the late 1930s.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke argues that Bomber Command's influence led the Air Ministry to deprioritize fighters, Army cooperation, Coastal Command, and the Fleet Air Arm until the late 1930s. Centralized aviation expertise could have worked if the ministry had understood the needs of each operator rather than treating one faction's priorities as universal. In practice, naval practitioners faced too many intermediaries before they could speak directly with aeronautical engineers. Wartime reform brought operators and designers into closer contact, while the lecture traces part of the earlier cultural divide to the Royal Flying Corps' treatment of engineering work. The lesson returns to Taranto because easy night handling and navigation were fleet requirements that aircraft designers had to understand in operational terms.

evidence.note: The lecture connects bomber-first priorities and Royal Flying Corps culture to the operator-engineer communication gap and Taranto's night-strike requirements.

segments.title: Swordfish reliability and shallow-water torpedo attacks
segments.summary: The Swordfish combined maintainability, forgiving night handling, and a specialized torpedo-dropping system suited to Taranto's shallow harbor.
segments.body: Eagle and Illustrious could draw on a large, repairable stock of Swordfish airframes, including stored machines and floatplanes that could be converted back to deck use. Their design emphasized easy operation at night so crews could devote attention to navigation while carrying torpedoes. A tension wire unspooled during the drop to stabilize the weapon and limit its dive after entering the water. That shallow-water control was separate from the duplex contact and magnetic fuzes that could still fail after a good entry. Five of the eleven British torpedoes hit their targets, and only two buried themselves in the harbour bottom. The lecture contrasts that controlled entry with the diving problems that reduced Japanese torpedo effectiveness at Pearl Harbor.

evidence.note: The lecture covers Swordfish availability, maintainability, night handling, and the mechanism stabilizing aerial torpedoes in shallow water.

segments.title: The original two-carrier Taranto strike
segments.summary: Before Eagle became unavailable, the plan called for two waves totaling forty-two Swordfish from two flight decks rather than the historical twenty-one aircraft.
segments.body: Each planned twenty-one-aircraft wave allocated twelve Swordfish to torpedoes, six to bombs, and three to flares, almost doubling the historical attacking force. Eagle's accumulated mechanical problems removed her shortly before the operation after improvised repairs could no longer keep her available. Her best serviceable Swordfish were transferred to Illustrious, reducing the plan from two flight decks to one. The setback also illustrates why British doctrine preferred paired carriers: two flight decks provided redundancy for launching, recovery, fighter cover, and damage repair during operations far from major dockyards.

evidence.note: The transcript gives the original forty-two-aircraft plan, Eagle's failure, and the survivability logic of paired flight decks.

segments.title: Three navies, three reasons for multi-carrier operations
segments.summary: British, American, and Japanese carrier concentration looked similar in practice but grew from different operational problems.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke distinguishes three interwar paths toward multi-carrier operations. Japan sought to coordinate strikes inside an attritional campaign plan, while the United States emphasized offensive scouting and damaging raids. Britain concentrated on keeping a carrier force and its flight decks operating despite battle damage and the immense distance between the South China Sea and home repair yards. Facilities in Australia, Singapore, and India could support some work but did not equal Britain's industrial base. The comparison helps explain why British armour, paired deployments, maintainability, and forward repair capacity formed one connected doctrine rather than separate design preferences.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts Japanese attritional strike coordination, American offensive scouting, and British carrier-force survivability across distant theaters.

segments.title: Operation Judgement inside Operation MB8
segments.summary: The Taranto attack was one objective inside a theatre-wide movement that reinforced the Mediterranean Fleet, carried stores, covered convoys, and raided the Strait of Otranto.
segments.body: Operation Judgement was one objective inside the much larger Operation MB8 schedule. Force F was to reinforce the Mediterranean Fleet from Gibraltar and carry stores for Malta while Illustrious and Eagle launched every available torpedo-spotter-reconnaissance aircraft against Taranto. The plan also covered convoys among Egypt, Malta, Crete, and Greece and sent light forces against traffic bound for Albania through the Strait of Otranto. Nesting the air strike inside reinforcement and supply movements gave the British fleet several reasons to be at sea while multiplying the demands on Italian situational awareness.

evidence.note: The transcript sets Operation Judgement within MB8's reinforcement, supply, convoy-cover, and Strait of Otranto objectives.

segments.title: Unexpected directions in Mediterranean raiding
segments.summary: The Otranto raid, Cape Bon, and the Italian attack on Alexandria show both navies exploiting directions and methods their opponents were least prepared to face.
segments.body: British cruisers and destroyers emerged from the Adriatic side of the Strait of Otranto to attack an escorted Italian merchant convoy from an unexpected direction. Dr. Clarke compares that shock with the later Battle of Cape Bon, where Royal Navy destroyers approached Italian light cruisers from the shoreward side. The pattern was not one-sided: Italian forces later struck British ships inside Alexandria harbour. Together the examples show an Anglo-Italian contest in which operational surprise often came from violating the defender's assumptions about where an attack could originate.

evidence.note: The lecture compares the Otranto convoy attack with Cape Bon and the later Italian attack inside Alexandria harbour.

segments.title: Operation MB8 as a fleet logistics system
segments.summary: Operation Judgment sat inside the much larger MB8 movement of battle fleets, reinforcements, troops, stores, convoys, and raiding forces.
segments.body: Operation MB8 moved a battle fleet, reinforcements, troop transports, stores, and several convoys through the central and eastern Mediterranean. Ajax and Sydney carried troops and guns to Souda Bay, while Orion transported Royal Air Force personnel to Athens. Merchant ships sailed among Alexandria, Port Said, Malta, Crete, and Greece under cruiser, destroyer, and escort protection. The force list shows that sustaining several garrisons and campaigns required many interlocking movements rather than a single convoy. Operation Judgement therefore depended on a theatre logistics system that could create an offensive opportunity without abandoning routine reinforcement and supply.

evidence.note: The transcript lists MB8 battle-fleet, troop, Royal Air Force, merchant-shipping, and convoy movements.

segments.title: Taranto's defenses and the risks faced by Swordfish crews
segments.summary: Leaking auxiliary fuel tanks, heavy anti-aircraft fire, missing barrage balloons, and incomplete torpedo nets shaped the extraordinary risk and opportunity at Taranto.
segments.body: Torpedo-carrying Swordfish needed long-range tanks fitted in the observer's cockpit, and some observers flew into tracer fire while standing in leaked aviation fuel. Taranto possessed 101 anti-aircraft guns and nearly 200 machine guns, but storms had removed many barrage balloons. Less than a third of the required anti-torpedo netting was rigged, and some nets were shallow enough for British torpedoes to pass beneath them. Illustrious maintained radio silence during the night recovery, so returning crews could not learn how many aircraft had survived while approaching the carrier. Nearly every crew believed it had been among the only survivors until its Swordfish descended on the lift and the brightly lit hangar revealed the other aircraft and aircrew.

evidence.note: The transcript describes leaking fuel tanks, harbour defences, incomplete nets and balloons, radio-silent recovery, and returning crews' surprise at the low losses.

segments.title: Historical damage and Taranto's operational payoff
segments.summary: Five torpedo hits disabled three Italian battleships, buying the Royal Navy time without permanently eliminating the Regia Marina.
segments.body: Conte di Cavour, Caio Duilio, and Littorio suffered major underwater damage, and Cavour never returned to Italian service. Delayed permission to beach Cavour may have allowed flooding to worsen, while Duilio was saved by being run aground. Updated British intelligence on anchorages, nets, and approach tracks helped a very small force place its weapons effectively. Dr. Clarke cautions against describing Taranto, even when combined with Cape Matapan, as the destruction of the Italian fleet, which remained a dangerous force. He also notes that Ark Royal was conducting a diversion elsewhere and that a stronger Skua dive-bomber component could have improved the bomb attack. The payoff was temporary operational freedom and a more manageable Mediterranean balance, achieved by only twenty-one attacking aircraft.

evidence.note: The lecture details damage to three battleships, the limited duration of the advantage, and the continuing capability of the Regia Marina.

segments.title: The unrealized two-carrier damage case
segments.summary: Even the original Eagle-Illustrious plan might have doubled the historical torpedo hits and permanently disabled more Italian battleships.
segments.body: The historical strike scored five hits from eleven torpedoes, so the planned forty-two-aircraft attack offers a useful intermediate counterfactual before the four-carrier scenario. Allowing for several unserviceable aircraft still leaves about twenty torpedoes in the two waves. Dr. Clarke conservatively projects roughly ten hits, with Vittorio Veneto and already damaged ships presenting plausible targets. Giulio Cesare's protected anchorage made her difficult to reach by torpedo, so concentrating Skua dive bombers offered the more plausible route to damaging her. Repeated hits could have turned temporary damage into permanent losses even without assembling four carriers.

evidence.note: The lecture scales the historical hit rate to the original forty-two-aircraft plan and identifies likely additional battleship damage.

segments.title: The 1942 rearmament horizon and Churchill's carrier pause
segments.summary: Britain planned naval procurement around a 1942 war horizon, but the early-war escort emergency interrupted capital-ship and carrier construction.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke places the shortage of British carriers inside the wider rearmament timeline. The Ten Year Rule ended in 1932, substantial funding became available in 1937, and the Royal Navy ordered long-lead ships for a war expected around 1942. An escort ordered in 1939 could take roughly eighteen months to enter service and still appear comfortably before that assumed deadline. When war arrived three years early, Churchill applied a 1914-style pause to capital ships, cruisers, and carriers while pressing for rapid escort construction. The lecture argues that many escorts had already been ordered and challenges Churchill's later presentation of himself as the person who initiated work already under way. The fleet's apparent lateness therefore reflected an incorrect strategic deadline as much as procurement failure.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses Churchill's construction pause, the escort emergency, the end of the Ten Year Rule, renewed funding, and planning for war in 1942.

segments.title: Two plausible routes to a four-carrier force
segments.summary: The counterfactual can preserve Courageous and Glorious or accelerate Formidable and redeploy Ark Royal to join Eagle and Illustrious.
segments.body: One route changes the losses of Courageous and Glorious so the older strike carriers survive for Mediterranean service. Courageous might take damaging rather than fatal torpedo hits, while Glorious could remain with the fleet or maintain an airborne patrol before encountering Scharnhorst. The other route completes Formidable roughly two months early and sends her east with Ark Royal, temporarily stripping the western basin of carrier cover. Hybrid combinations could preserve one older ship and add either Ark Royal or Formidable as the fourth deck. Dr. Clarke treats the survival of the older ships as the easier change because comparatively small changes to their historical losses can keep them available.

evidence.note: The transcript develops the Courageous-Glorious and Ark Royal-Formidable alternatives and explains their plausibility.

segments.title: Four-carrier air groups and maintenance mass
segments.summary: More carriers create not only a larger air group but a shared pool of fitters, spare parts, transport aircraft, and serviceable machines.
segments.body: The older-carrier option could assemble about 114 Swordfish and 36 Fulmars, while Ark Royal and Formidable introduce Skuas and Albacores. Formidable's likely early group draws on 826 and 829 Naval Air Squadrons, which helps explain why new Albacores appear in that route. Exact serviceability remains uncertain, but four ships concentrate maintainers and spares that can be exchanged between decks and shore bases. Swordfish could ferry parts between carriers and Malta, turning the air group itself into part of the maintenance network. This logistical mass makes a fuller strike more credible than simply multiplying each carrier's nominal complement.

evidence.note: The lecture estimates the alternative air groups and explains how shared personnel and spares improve aircraft generation.

segments.title: Organizing a three-wave night strike
segments.summary: British doctrine points toward three roughly forty-aircraft waves, using Fulmars for illumination and concentrating Swordfish on torpedo attack.
segments.body: Sending every aircraft at once would overcrowd the dark harbour and leave formations circling too long while assembling. Half-hour-separated waves let each carrier contribute roughly a squadron while preserving room to manoeuvre. Fulmars could drop flares and attack barrage balloons, freeing Swordfish for torpedoes and bombs. Skuas and Albacores would probably emphasize bombing because their crews had less experience with the specialized night torpedo role. Surviving doctrine is fragmentary, so the exact mix remains a reconstruction rather than a documented order. A rule of roughly one squadron per carrier nevertheless produces the forty-to-forty-eight-aircraft formations reflected in British night exercises and planning.

evidence.note: The transcript lays out three waves, formation constraints, Fulmar flare duties, likely weapon allocation, and the fragmentary basis for reconstructing doctrine.

segments.title: Twenty-five torpedo hits against Italian protection
segments.summary: A conservative projection of twenty-five hits from sixty or more torpedoes creates repeated-hit casualties beyond what Italian underwater protection was designed to absorb.
segments.body: Applying a lower hit rate than the historical attack still produces roughly twenty-five successes from sixty or more torpedoes. Some weapons would be directed against cruisers, while Duilio, Littorio, Vittorio Veneto, and other exposed battleships could receive repeated hits. Twenty-five hits across a limited target set make multi-hit casualties plausible even under conservative assumptions. The Pugliese underwater-protection system could mitigate individual explosions on some battleships, but not every ship carried it and the system was not designed for this concentration of damage.

evidence.note: The lecture derives a conservative twenty-five-hit case and explains why repeated hits would exceed the protection available across the target fleet.

segments.title: Flare silhouettes and Italian anti-aircraft endurance
segments.summary: Repeated waves exploit changing Italian ammunition readiness while twelve flare aircraft silhouette the fleet and keep attackers comparatively dark.
segments.body: The first wave reaches a surprised defence, while the second faces guns that have found their rhythm and is likely to meet the heaviest fire. By the third wave, however, Italian positions that historically fired about twelve thousand rounds may be running short of ammunition. Defenders withheld their searchlights because illuminating the harbour could also expose their own ships and deepen the contrast in which aircraft could hide. British flare aircraft instead lit the water behind the anchored ships, outlining targets without placing the torpedo bombers in the brightest part of the scene. Expanding from four flare aircraft to twelve would intensify that geometry and make it harder for Italian gunners to distinguish attackers against the darkness.

evidence.note: The lecture compares defensive readiness across three waves and explains how rearward flares silhouette ships while reducing contrast on attacking aircraft.

segments.title: Eight targets and overloaded Taranto repair
segments.summary: Eight exposed capital ships and heavy cruisers would spread pumps, salvage crews, and dockyard capacity across far more casualties than Taranto historically handled.
segments.body: With Duilio, Littorio, Vittorio Veneto, Conte di Cavour, Andrea Doria, and the heavy cruisers Gorizia, Zara, and Fiume exposed, Dr. Clarke counts eight good torpedo targets. Two to four hits on each selected ship would sink some hulls outright in the harbour. Taranto's port facilities were already overloaded by the historical casualty list. A much broader set of damaged ships would divide pumps, repair personnel, and dockyard resources so severely that otherwise salvageable vessels could become permanent losses.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies eight exposed targets and connects multiple sinkings to the historical limits of Taranto's repair facilities.

segments.title: Taranto as a twenty-year set-piece operation
segments.summary: Taranto succeeded because the Royal Navy finally executed a harbor strike it had studied, rehearsed, and equipped for across two decades.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke rejects the idea that Taranto was an improvised piece of luck. The Royal Navy had studied harbor attacks since the First World War, developed night-strike doctrine, gathered the necessary intelligence, and built aircraft suited to the task. Italian resistance was serious, but the British controlled the timing and form of a set-piece operation that matched their preparation. The watch point is useful for understanding how doctrine, procurement, intelligence, and training combine before tactical success becomes visible in battle.

evidence.note: The transcript characterizes Taranto as a meticulously planned set-piece operation prepared for over roughly twenty years with aircraft ideal for the mission.

segments.title: The Italian battlefleet after a larger Taranto
segments.summary: With most battleships and several heavy cruisers disabled, Italy might avoid Cape Spartivento and lose its major surface threat for about a year.
segments.body: Bombers might attack fuel installations, cruisers in Mar Piccolo, or battleships that were difficult to reach by torpedo, although their results are less predictable. Dr. Clarke's severe case leaves Giulio Cesare as the only viable battleship while repair facilities concentrate on Littorio and Vittorio Veneto. Those newer ships would probably return, but the older dreadnoughts could become constructive total losses after prolonged submergence and water damage. The constraint is not simply material resources: dockyard space, salvage capacity, and time would all be scarce at once. A fleet reduced to one older battleship and fewer heavy cruisers would have little incentive to contest a British force containing Renown and Ark Royal. Cape Spartivento might therefore never occur in recognizable form.

evidence.note: The transcript projects extensive non-operational ships, limited repair capacity, and a radically altered Cape Spartivento decision.

segments.title: Mediterranean force deployment after Taranto
segments.summary: Removing the Italian capital-ship threat frees British heavy units and carrier capacity for Malta, Crete, the Atlantic, or the Far East.
segments.body: The historical Regia Marina could assemble a surface force much larger than Germany's and repeatedly pressed British operations. At Cape Spartivento, Italy fielded two battleships, six heavy cruisers, and fourteen destroyers, a concentration the Kriegsmarine could scarcely imagine after its losses around Norway. If that threat disappears, a Revenge-class battleship or Renown may be sufficient for local deterrence, allowing stronger units to move elsewhere. Continued access to three carriers in theatre could also provide more fighters, spares, and operational decks during the campaign for Crete. The counterfactual therefore changes not only battles but the allocation and readiness of British forces across the Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Far East. The comparison also restores the Regia Marina's scale to a discussion that often treats Germany as the only consequential Axis navy.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts Italian and German fleet strength and discusses British battleship, carrier, and theatre redeployment.

segments.title: Convoys, the Afrika Korps, and Crete
segments.summary: Without Italian heavy escorts, Axis reinforcement convoys become more vulnerable and small changes in delivery rates could reshape North Africa and Crete.
segments.body: The defeat of the Italian Tenth Army in Operation Compass made German reinforcement urgent, but the sea route depended partly on heavy Regia Marina protection. Stronger British surface forces could intercept more convoys or force less efficient routing, reducing the supplies available to Erwin Rommel and the Afrika Korps. Even modest changes in convoy arrivals could matter because long campaigns turn on accumulated transport and supply losses. The same maritime imbalance might prevent Italian amphibious reinforcement of Crete and let Britain sustain a stronger position in North Africa. Dr. Clarke emphasizes that the chain of consequences becomes increasingly uncertain and ultimately depends on how effectively Britain exploits the temporary advantage.

evidence.note: The transcript connects missing Italian heavy escorts to Axis convoy losses, Afrika Korps reinforcement, North African operations, and Crete.

segments.title: Surviving carriers, Crete, and Force Z
segments.summary: Keeping Courageous and Glorious alive could leave older carriers in the Mediterranean, preserve newer ships for the Atlantic, and provide a flight deck for Force Z.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke returns to the survival of Courageous and Glorious as the likeliest route to the four-carrier strike. Their continued Mediterranean service could reduce pressure on newer carriers and sustain more fighters, spares, and operational decks around Crete. Leaving the older ships in that theatre could preserve newer carriers for the North Atlantic. If either survivor remained available when Force Z formed, the older carrier could accompany the battleships in the Far East and provide the air component the historical force lacked. The counterfactual still depends on Courageous surviving torpedo damage and Glorious not separating from support without an airborne patrol.

evidence.note: The lecture discusses surviving older carriers, Crete, Atlantic deployment, Force Z, and the conditions needed to prevent the historical losses.

segments.title: Glorious, command culture, and Harwood
segments.summary: Royal Navy memory of First World War command failures makes Glorious theories that require many officers to disregard separate chains of command less plausible.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke is skeptical of explanations for Glorious's movements that require several officers to disregard different chains of command at once. The interwar Royal Navy remembered the losses caused when officers freelanced during the First World War and had strong institutional reasons to punish similar behaviour. Political favour might still bring promotion, but the service could limit an officer's influence through a distant or unimportant appointment. The lecture invokes Henry Harwood after the Battle of the River Plate as a warning about how blame from the Royal Air Force and Army could damage a naval officer's position. This command-culture test makes the counterfactual more rigorous by asking whether a proposed divergence fits the institutions and incentives of the period.

evidence.note: The transcript tests Glorious theories against Royal Navy command culture and uses Harwood to illustrate blame and career consequences.

segments.title: Albacore and Skua reputations after Taranto
segments.summary: Participation in a larger Taranto strike could give the Albacore a celebrated debut and preserve the Skua's identity as a dive bomber.
segments.body: If Formidable joins the strike, the Albacore receives a highly visible combat debut even though Swordfish still perform most of the torpedo work. Skua bombing success could likewise make the aircraft better remembered for the dive-bomber role it was designed to perform. The lecture notes that presenting the Skua as a fighter helped move it through the Air Ministry procurement system, obscuring that intended role. A strong showing by both types might increase support for an earlier British dive-bomber successor. The closing prompt asks viewers to choose among the counterfactual routes but does not contain a transcript-visible answer.

evidence.note: The transcript links a larger Taranto strike to Albacore and Skua reputations, procurement framing, and possible successor development.
